claims.text: Where a Nigerian company declares dividend out of profits on which no tax is payable because there are no total profits, or because total profits are less than the dividend declared, the company paying the dividend is charged to tax.

The charge is at the rate prescribed in section 56 of the Act, as if the dividend were the total profits of the company for the year of assessment to which the accounts, out of which the dividend is declared, relate.
This rule applies whether or not the recipient of the dividend is a Nigerian company.
The rule does not apply to dividends declared out of retained earnings, to the extent that the profits or gains in the retained earnings have been taxed under the Act.
The rule does not apply to dividends declared out of profits or gains that are exempt from income tax by the Act.
The rule does not apply to franked investment income as provided in the Act.

The rule does not apply to distributions by a real estate investment company to its shareholders from rental income and dividend income received on behalf of those shareholders, whether paid out of profits of the year in which the dividend is declared or of previous reporting periods.

gaps: The rate in section 56 is not among the passages, so the rate cannot be stated.
Whether the company's own dividend falls within any exception depends on facts about its profits that the question does not give.
The passages do not state how any tax deducted at source on the dividend under section 51 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 interacts with this charge.

claims.text: Where a non-resident person makes taxable supplies from outside Nigeria to persons in Nigeria, the taxable person to whom the supply is made in Nigeria shall withhold the VAT due on the supply and remit it to the Service.
A non-resident person who makes taxable supplies to Nigeria shall register for tax and include VAT on its invoice for all taxable supplies.
The Service may, by notice, appoint any person, including a non-resident supplier, to collect the VAT and remit it to the Service.

Where the supplier has been appointed in this way and has made a taxable supply to a taxable person in Nigeria, that taxable person does not have the obligation to withhold the VAT, except where the appointed person has failed to collect the VAT.

The Service may direct a taxable person to whom a taxable supply is made in Nigeria, and who is issued an invoice on which VAT is not included, to self-account for the VAT payable and remit it to the Service.

VAT collected, withheld or self-accounted under section 155 is to be remitted to the Service on or before the 14th day of the month immediately following the month of the transaction, or as may be prescribed by the Service.

The remission must be accompanied by a schedule showing the name, Tax ID and address of the contractor or supplier, invoice number, gross amount of invoice, amount of the VAT and the month to which the return relates.
A non-resident person that makes a taxable supply to a person in Nigeria may appoint a representative for the purpose of compliance with its VAT obligations.

gaps: The passages do not say whether software services are a taxable supply.
The passages do not say whether the foreign online company is a non-resident person, or whether the Service has appointed it to collect VAT.
The passages do not say whether the payer is a taxable person.
The passages do not say whether the payer is a person who must withhold under section 155(1), such as a government body or a person appointed by the Service.

That definition says any business providing professional services shall not be classified as a small company.

Under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, tax on the total profits of a small company is levied at 0%, and any other company is taxed at the rate of 30 per cent from the commencement of the Act.

claims.text: Where the relevant tax authority discovers or is of the opinion that a taxable person has not been assessed, or was assessed at less than ought to have been charged, it may assess the person for the amount or additional amount, within six years of the assessment.
The six-year limit does not stop the relevant tax authority from continuing a tax audit and raising an additional assessment where the audit started before the six years expired.

Despite the time limit in subsection (1), where there is a deliberate misstatement by a taxable person in connection with any tax under the Nigeria Tax Act, 2025 or any other tax law, the relevant tax authority may at any time, and as often as necessary, assess the person to make good any loss of tax attributable to the deliberate misstatement.
All relevant facts are considered in working out the additional tax, even where they were not known when an earlier assessment or additional assessment was made for the same year.

Section 41 does not prevent the tax authority from making an assessment or additional assessment for a year if it does not involve re-opening an issue on the same facts that was determined for that year under section 41(5) by agreement or on appeal.

gaps: The passages do not say how the six years in section 36(1) are counted beyond the words 'within six years of the assessment', so no end date is worked out here.

questions.question: My company made ₦120 million profit this year. How much company income tax will it pay?

claims.text: Tax is levied for each year of assessment on the total profits of every company, at 0% for a small company.
Tax on any other company is levied at the rate of 30 per cent from the commencement of the Act.

The total profits of a company are its total assessable profits from all sources, including chargeable gains, less any loss ascertained under subsection (6) and capital allowance under Part I of the First Schedule.

A company must include dividend income in its profits, gross of any tax paid or deducted at source. Dividends a Nigerian company receives by way of shares of the paying company are not included in its profits chargeable to tax.

Where a company's effective tax rate for a year of assessment is less than 15%, it must recompute and pay additional tax to bring the rate to 15%. This applies to a constituent entity of an MNE group and to any other company with aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 and above in the relevant year of assessment.

gaps: The passages do not say whether the company is a small company, and do not define a small company, so the applicable rate (0% or 30 per cent) cannot be determined.
The passages do not say whether the ₦120 million is total profits after losses and capital allowances, or whether it includes chargeable gains or dividends, so the taxable base is unknown.
The passages do not give the company's turnover or say whether it is part of an MNE group, so whether the 15% effective tax rate rule applies is unknown.
Applying a rate to ₦120 million is a calculation, and it is not done here.
Subsection (6) of section 27 on losses is not among the passages.

Where a company's effective tax rate for a year of assessment is less than 15%, it must recompute and pay additional tax to bring the rate to 15%. This applies to a constituent entity of an MNE group and to any other company with aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 and above in the relevant year of assessment. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57]

- The passages do not say whether the ₦120 million is total profits after losses and capital allowances, or whether it includes chargeable gains or dividends, so the taxable base is unknown.

- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56 (gazette page A 426)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4) (gazette pages A 412, A 413)

- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57 (gazette page A 426)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4): The National Assembly text requires companies in the priority sector to obtain a certificate of acceptance from the Industrial Inspectorate Department for qualifying capital expenditure; the gazette has no such condition. (DR-039)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8: Cross-reference: the gazette cites section 51 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, the National Assembly text section 50. (DR-007, DR-008)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The minimum tax is measured differently. Gazette: covered tax paid divided by profits, where profits are net profit before tax less 5% of depreciation and personnel cost. National Assembly: covered taxes (companies income tax, petroleum profit tax, hydrocarbon tax, development levy, priority sector tax credit) as a percentage of net income, which excludes franked investment income and unrealised gains or losses. (DR-051)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette applies the 15% minimum to every constituent entity of an MNE group; the National Assembly text only where the group's turnover is at least 750 million (printed with a pound sign) or its equivalent. (DR-052)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The 15% minimum effective tax rate applies from an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 in the gazette and ₦50,000,000,000 in the National Assembly text. (DR-053)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The National Assembly text exempts approved free-zone enterprises (except for sales into the customs territory and MNE entities) and lets the Service set a higher turnover threshold by regulation; the gazette has neither and measures turnover in the relevant year of assessment rather than the financial year. (DR-054)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette numbers the subsections (1), (2) and (4), with no (3); the labels are kept as printed. The National Assembly text has (1) to (4). (DR-055)
